formulas.name: Adjacency matrix (Harary 1969; Biggs 1974)
formulas.where: Entry \((u,v)\) counts the edges from \(u\) to \(v\) (sums their weights). variants.gm_adjacency: Dense or sparse matrix of the edge counts or weights; weights replace counts, directed edges fill one entry, undirected edges two, and an undirected loop one entry (or two under the doubling convention).

formulas.name: Bethe Hessian (Saade et al. 2014)
formulas.where: Symmetric matrix defined for any real \(r\); the negative eigenvalues of \(H(r_c)\) count the communities in the spectral method of the paper. \(r_c\) depends on the degree sequence.

variants.gm_bethe_hessian: The matrix \(H(r)\) at the default \(r\) of the tool or a chosen \(r\); weights enter through \(A\) and the strength in \(D\).

Parallel edges add to \(A\) and \(D\); the paper defines the matrix for simple graphs.

networkx.behaviour: NetworkX does not implement the Bethe Hessian for multigraphs.

formulas.name: Unoriented incidence matrix (Bondy and Murty 2008)

formulas.name: Oriented incidence matrix
formulas.where: \(-1\) at the source and \(+1\) at the target of each edge; \(BB^{\top}=D-A_{\text{sym}}\) is the combinatorial Laplacian of the underlying undirected graph.

formulas.name: Biadjacency matrix
formulas.latex: m_{pq}=\text{number (or total weight) of edges between }p\in P\text{ and }q\in Q
formulas.where: The part of the adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph that joins the two classes; it has \(|P|\) rows and \(|Q|\) columns, so it is not square in general.

variants.gm_incidence: Node-by-edge matrix: unoriented 0/1 for undirected input, signed for directed input; the biadjacency variant is node-class by node-class for two-mode input. Columns follow the order of the edge list.

formulas.name: Combinatorial Laplacian (Biggs 1974; Chung 1997)
formulas.where: Symmetric, positive semidefinite for undirected input with non-negative weights; row sums are 0. For directed input \(L=D_{\text{out}}-A\) is the usual extension (out-degree Laplacian); it is not symmetric.

formulas.name: Normalized Laplacian (Chung 1997)
formulas.where: Entries \(1\) on the diagonal, \(-1/\sqrt{d_ud_v}\) for adjacent nodes. Chung sets the diagonal entry to 0 for a node of degree 0, which makes the formula defined with isolated nodes.

formulas.name: Random-walk Laplacian
formulas.where: Defined only when every degree (out-degree) is positive; rows sum to 0.

variants.gm_laplacian: The Laplacian family: combinatorial \(D-A\), normalized \(I-D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\) and random-walk \(I-D^{-1}A\) forms, each with unit or edge weights in \(A\); for directed input the degree is the out-degree (row sum) in the combinatorial form, and other directed normalizations (symmetrized by the stationary distribution) are different matrices.
variants.cat_laplacian_magnetic_matrix: Magnetic Laplacian of a directed graph. The sources know it by name only (a documented-only tool entry) and give no formula.

formulas.name: Modularity matrix (Newman 2006)
formulas.where: Observed minus expected tie weight under the configuration null model; needs \(m>0\).

formulas.name: Directed modularity matrix (Leicht and Newman 2008)
formulas.where: Out-degree of the source times in-degree of the target, divided by \(m\).

variants.gm_modularity: Undirected form with \(k_uk_v/2m\) or directed form with \(k^{\text{out}}_uk^{\text{in}}_v/m\); weighted input replaces degrees by strengths and \(m\) by the total weight.

edge_cases.definition_gives: \(n=0\): the 0\(\times\)0 matrix; there is no \(m\) to divide by, but there are no entries either.
\(m=0\): the expected term \(k_uk_v/2m\) is 0/0, so the matrix is not defined.
A loop adds to \(a_{uu}\) and to \(k_u\) (by 1 or 2 per the adjacency convention); the formula does not decide the convention.
Parallel edges add to \(a_{uv}\), \(k\) and \(m\).

networkx.behaviour: NetworkX does not implement the modularity matrices for multigraphs.

formulas.name: Bandwidth (Cuthill and McKee 1969)
formulas.where: Largest distance from the diagonal of a non-zero entry of \(A\) when rows and columns are ordered by \(\pi\); orderings such as reverse Cuthill-McKee try to make it small. Minimizing it over all \(\pi\) is hard, so tools return a heuristic ordering.

variants.matrix_bandwidth: Collective entry for sparse-matrix orderings and their bandwidth and wavefront; the bandwidth is written above.

formulas.name: Eigenpairs of a symmetric matrix (Golub and Van Loan 2013)
formulas.where: A real symmetric \(M\) has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal set of eigenvectors; each \(x_i\) is determined up to sign, and up to rotation within an eigenspace when \(\lambda_i\) is repeated. A non-symmetric \(M\) (directed input) can have complex eigenpairs.

variants.eigenvectors_matrix: Eigenvectors of any of the graph matrices; which matrix, how many vectors, the ordering of eigenvalues and the sign rule are properties of the tool.

edge_cases.definition_gives: Repeated eigenvalues make the eigenvectors non-unique (any orthonormal basis of the eigenspace); a sign flip is always allowed, so two correct results can differ by sign.
A non-symmetric matrix has right and left eigenvectors that differ, and possibly complex ones.

formulas.name: Estrada index (sum of subgraph centralities; Estrada and Rodriguez-Velazquez 2005)
formulas.where: Weighted count of closed walks of every length (\(\operatorname{tr}\,A^k/k!\) summed over \(k\)); always defined, since the series converges for every finite \(A\). Subgraph centrality of \(u\) is \((e^{A})_{uu}\).

variants.estrada_index: The sum \(\operatorname{tr}\,e^{A}\) of the exponentials of the adjacency eigenvalues; a variant over another matrix (Laplacian) is a different index.

edge_cases.definition_gives: \(n=0\): empty sum, 0 (and \(\operatorname{tr}\,e^{A}=0\) for the 0\(\times\)0 matrix).
Loops put entries on the diagonal of \(A\) and change the spectrum; the definition does not exclude them.
The eigenvalue form needs a symmetric \(A\); \(\operatorname{tr}\,e^{A}\) is defined for directed input too (real part when eigenvalues are complex).

formulas.name: Algebraic connectivity (Fiedler 1973)
formulas.where: The second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue; positive exactly when the graph is connected (\(n\ge 2\)). The Fiedler vector is orthogonal to the constant vector and is unique up to sign when \(\mu_2\) is simple.

formulas.name: Normalized form
formulas.where: Same definition with the normalized Laplacian; the eigenvector then lives on the \(D^{1/2}\)-scaled space.

variants.gm_fiedler: Value \(\mu_2\) (algebraic connectivity) or the vector \(f\); combinatorial or normalized Laplacian; the spectral bisection splits nodes by the sign of \(f\).

edge_cases.definition_gives: \(n=0\): no eigenvalues; not defined.
\(n=1\): there is no second eigenvalue; not defined.

a graph matrix (adjacency, Laplacian, normalized Laplacian)

formulas.name: Spectrum of a graph (Biggs 1974; Chung 1997)
formulas.where: The multiset of eigenvalues of the chosen matrix; real for a symmetric \(M\). Which matrix is meant (adjacency spectrum, Laplacian spectrum, normalized-Laplacian spectrum) changes the result completely.

variants.graph_spectrum: Eigenvalues of the adjacency, Laplacian or normalized Laplacian matrix, sorted ascending or descending; which one is returned is a property of the tool and its options.

edge_cases.definition_gives: \(n=0\): the empty multiset.
Adjacency and Laplacian spectra are all 0; the normalized Laplacian spectrum is all 0 by Chung's convention.
A non-symmetric matrix can have complex eigenvalues; the real spectral theory holds for undirected input.
Multiplicities matter: the spectrum is a multiset, and repeated eigenvalues are expected (for example, a complete graph has one large eigenvalue and \(n-1\) equal ones).

spectral_gap.note: The tool function is known by name only; which matrix it uses is not recorded, so both published forms are given.

notation.meaning: graph with node set \(V\) and edge set \(E\); every edge has a source and a target (the two ends of an undirected edge are interchangeable)

formulas.name: Spectral gap of a regular graph (Hoory, Linial and Wigderson 2006)
formulas.where: For a \(d\)-regular graph the difference between the largest adjacency eigenvalue \(\lambda_1=d\) and the second; equal to \(\mu_2\) of the Laplacian \(dI-A\), so it coincides with the algebraic connectivity.

formulas.name: Laplacian gap
formulas.where: For non-regular graphs the gap is usually taken as the algebraic connectivity \(\mu_2\) of the Laplacian; the adjacency form \(\lambda_1-\lambda_2\) is a different number.

variants.cat_gap_spectral: The gap between the first two eigenvalues; whether the tool uses the adjacency, Laplacian or normalized Laplacian is not recorded.

edge_cases.definition_gives: \(\mu_2=0\): the Laplacian gap is 0; the adjacency gap \(\lambda_1-\lambda_2\) is 0 when two components share the largest eigenvalue.
\(n<2\): there is no second eigenvalue; not defined.
